blocks.content: Imagine a busy kitchen where chefs keep placing finished dishes on a small pass through counter, and waiters keep picking dishes up from that same counter to serve them.

The counter only holds so many plates. If the chefs get too far ahead, the counter fills up and they have to pause. If the waiters get too far ahead, the counter goes empty and they have to wait for the next dish.

This everyday picture is exactly the producer consumer problem in concurrent programming. One or more threads produce items, one or more threads consume them, and they share a common buffer in between.

Getting this coordination wrong is one of the most common sources of subtle concurrency bugs, so this lesson walks through the naive broken approach first, then builds up to the correct patterns used in real systems.
The producer consumer problem asks how independent producer and consumer threads can safely share a bounded buffer without racing each other, losing items, or corrupting shared state.
1. Setting up the problem
A producer consumer system has three moving parts. Producer threads generate items and push them somewhere. Consumer threads pull items from that same place and process them.
The third part is the shared buffer sitting between them. It is usually a queue with a fixed capacity, which is why this is often called the bounded buffer problem.
Why a buffer at all
Without a buffer, a producer would have to hand an item directly to a consumer and wait for it to be accepted, which ties the two together tightly and kills throughput.
A buffer decouples the two sides. Producers can run ahead when consumers are briefly slow, and consumers can drain a backlog when producers pause.
Why bounded and not unlimited
An unlimited buffer sounds simpler, but it just moves the problem. If producers are consistently faster than consumers, an unbounded queue grows forever and eventually exhausts memory.

["Producers must pause when the buffer is full, this is called backpressure","Consumers must pause when the buffer is empty, there is nothing to do","The buffer itself must never be corrupted by concurrent access"]
items: Producers must pause when the buffer is full, this is called backpressure
Consumers must pause when the buffer is empty, there is nothing to do
The buffer itself must never be corrupted by concurrent access

blocks.title: Real world framing
blocks.content: Message queues, job schedulers, logging pipelines, and thread pools are all producer consumer systems at their core, just with different names for producer, consumer, and buffer.
2. The naive shared list approach
A tempting first attempt is to just use a plain list or array shared between threads, with producers appending and consumers removing.
This looks fine in a single threaded mental model, but multiple threads touching the same list at the same time is a recipe for a race condition.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512302536-808502918.png
blocks.alt: Two producers both reading the same buffer size, both deciding there is room, and both writing to the same slot so one item is silently lost

blocks.content: What actually goes wrong

Operations like checking the size, adding an element, and removing an element are each made of several smaller steps under the hood. When two threads interleave those steps, the list can end up in an inconsistent state.

["Two producers can both read the same size, both decide there is room, and both write, silently overwriting each other","A consumer can read stale size information and try to remove from an empty list, crashing or returning garbage","Items can be lost entirely because a write from one thread overwrites a write from another before it is read","The same item can be delivered to two different consumers because of a corrupted internal index"]
items: Two producers can both read the same size, both decide there is room, and both write, silently overwriting each other
A consumer can read stale size information and try to remove from an empty list, crashing or returning garbage
Items can be lost entirely because a write from one thread overwrites a write from another before it is read
The same item can be delivered to two different consumers because of a corrupted internal index

blocks.title: Why this is hard to catch
blocks.content: These bugs often do not show up in testing because they depend on precise timing between threads. They tend to appear only under production load, which makes them expensive to diagnose.

blocks.content: 3. The bounded buffer idea
The fix starts with recognizing that every operation on the shared buffer needs to be treated as one indivisible step, not a sequence of separate reads and writes.
A mutex or lock around the buffer state ensures only one thread can inspect or modify it at a time. That alone solves the corruption problem, but it does not solve waiting.
Locking is necessary but not sufficient
blocks.text: Locking is necessary but not sufficient

blocks.content: If a producer holds the lock and finds the buffer full, it cannot just spin forever holding the lock, because that would block every other thread, including consumers who could free up space.
The thread needs to release the lock, sleep until something changes, and reacquire the lock before checking again. This is exactly what condition variables provide.

{"headers":["Requirement","Naive list","Bounded buffer with lock and condition variable"],"rows":[["Prevents corrupted state","No","Yes"],["Producer waits when full","No, silently drops or overflows","Yes, blocks until space is free"],["Consumer waits when empty","No, returns null or crashes","Yes, blocks until an item arrives"],["Wakes waiting threads on change","No","Yes, via notify"]]}
4. Wait and notify coordination
The classic solution pairs a mutex with a condition variable, sometimes exposed in languages as wait, notify, and notifyAll, or as condition.wait and condition.notify.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512304291-643376554.png
blocks.alt: A producer acquiring the lock, waiting and releasing it when the buffer is full, then waking and rechecking after a consumer calls notify

blocks.content: The core rules

["A producer acquires the lock, then checks if the buffer is full","If full, the producer calls wait, which atomically releases the lock and sleeps","When a consumer removes an item, it calls notify to wake a sleeping producer","The woken producer reacquires the lock and rechecks the condition before proceeding","The same pattern applies symmetrically for consumers waiting on an empty buffer"]
items: A producer acquires the lock, then checks if the buffer is full
If full, the producer calls wait, which atomically releases the lock and sleeps
When a consumer removes an item, it calls notify to wake a sleeping producer
The woken producer reacquires the lock and rechecks the condition before proceeding
The same pattern applies symmetrically for consumers waiting on an empty buffer

blocks.content: Why the recheck matters

A thread that wakes up from wait must always recheck its condition in a loop, not just assume the world is now as it hoped. This protects against spurious wakeups and against another thread sneaking in first and taking the last slot or the last item.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content: Always wrap wait calls in a while loop that rechecks the condition, never in a plain if statement. This single habit prevents a large share of concurrency bugs.

blocks.title: Why notifyAll over notify
blocks.text: notify wakes exactly one waiting thread, chosen arbitrarily, which can be wrong if some waiters are producers and others are consumers on the same condition. notifyAll wakes everyone, and each rechecks its own while loop condition, so it is safer by default even though it wakes a few extra threads.

The diagram below shows two producers pushing into a bounded buffer of capacity five and two consumers draining it, with the wait states triggered at the full and empty edges.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494814049-779024583.png
blocks.alt: Producers and consumers around a bounded buffer, with wait states shown when the buffer is full or empty

blocks.content: When the buffer hits capacity, any producer trying to add another item moves into the waiting state instead of overwriting data or spinning uselessly.
Symmetrically, when the buffer is empty, consumers wait rather than reading garbage or busy looping on an empty check.

blocks.content: 7. Using a built in blocking queue instead
blocks.text: 7. Using a built in blocking queue instead

blocks.content: Writing your own lock and condition variable logic is a great learning exercise, but production code almost always reaches for a language provided blocking queue instead.

A blocking queue bakes in exactly the same semantics, a bounded capacity, producers blocking when full, consumers blocking when empty, but the implementation is tested, tuned, and far less error prone than a hand rolled version.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512305949-53157855.png
blocks.alt: Hand rolled mutex and condition variable code compared side by side with a built in blocking queue that provides the same bounded semantics internally

8. Common mistakes and pitfalls
Even with the right primitives, there are a handful of mistakes that show up again and again in producer consumer code.
Missed notifications
If a producer adds an item but forgets to call notify, a sleeping consumer may never wake up, even though data is sitting right there waiting to be read.
Using if instead of while

Checking the condition with if instead of a while loop means a thread that wakes up proceeds without rechecking, which can lead to consuming from an empty buffer if another thread grabbed the item first.
Spurious wakeups
Some platforms allow a waiting thread to wake up even when nobody called notify, due to implementation details of the underlying operating system. A while loop recheck protects against this for free.
Notify versus notifyAll confusion
Calling notify when multiple different conditions share one lock can wake the wrong kind of thread, leaving the correct one asleep indefinitely. This is sometimes called a lost wakeup.
Holding the lock too long
Doing slow work like network calls or file writes while still holding the buffer lock blocks every other thread unnecessarily. Copy the item out, release the lock, then do the slow work.

["Forgetting to notify after a state change that another thread is waiting on","Using if instead of while around a wait call","Assuming a woken thread has an up to date view of shared state without rechecking","Doing expensive work inside the critical section instead of just moving data in and out","Choosing notify when notifyAll is needed because multiple wait conditions share one lock"]
items: Forgetting to notify after a state change that another thread is waiting on
Using if instead of while around a wait call
Assuming a woken thread has an up to date view of shared state without rechecking
Doing expensive work inside the critical section instead of just moving data in and out
Choosing notify when notifyAll is needed because multiple wait conditions share one lock

blocks.title: Debugging tip
blocks.content: If a producer consumer system occasionally hangs under load but never crashes, suspect a missed notification or an if instead of while bug before anything else. These are the two most common causes of that exact symptom.
9. Multiple producers, multiple consumers, and fairness
blocks.text: 9. Multiple producers, multiple consumers, and fairness

blocks.content: Everything so far generalizes cleanly from one producer and one consumer to many of each, because the buffer, the lock, and the condition variables do not care how many threads are on either side.
Thundering herd

Calling notifyAll wakes every waiting thread, but only one of them can actually proceed, since only one slot or one item became available. The rest recheck their while loop, find nothing changed, and go back to sleep.
This is a small amount of wasted wakeup work, but it is usually a fine tradeoff for correctness, and most built in blocking queues handle it more efficiently internally.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512307874-594340705.png
blocks.alt: notifyAll waking every sleeping consumer when only one item is available, so only one consumer proceeds while the others recheck and sleep again

blocks.content: Fairness is not guaranteed by default
blocks.text: Fairness is not guaranteed by default

blocks.content: Standard condition variables typically do not guarantee that the longest waiting thread wakes first. If strict ordering matters, a fair lock or an explicit ticketing scheme is needed on top.

blocks.title: Scaling up producers and consumers
blocks.text: A logging system might have twenty application threads producing log lines and three background threads consuming and flushing them to disk. The same bounded buffer pattern applies unchanged, just with more threads on each side.

blocks.content: 10. Connecting this to real systems
The producer consumer pattern is not just an interview topic, it is the backbone of a huge amount of real infrastructure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512309643-543043389.png
blocks.alt: The producer consumer pattern branching out into real systems such as message queues, thread pool task queues, and logging pipelines

blocks.content: Message queues

Systems like Kafka, RabbitMQ, and SQS are producer consumer problems at a distributed scale, with the bounded buffer replaced by durable, partitioned storage, but the same full and empty backpressure ideas still apply.
Thread pools
A thread pool is a consumer side pattern where worker threads pull tasks from a shared blocking queue, and callers submitting tasks are effectively producers pushing into that same queue.
Logging and metrics pipelines

Application threads produce log lines or metric points faster than a disk or network sink can absorb them, so a bounded in memory queue smooths out the difference and applies backpressure when needed.
Once this pattern clicks, you start noticing it everywhere, from GPU job scheduling to video frame pipelines to the humble print spooler.
The core lesson holds across all of these: never let two threads touch shared mutable state without coordination, and always give both full and empty conditions a proper place to wait.
